entities.name: David Alopaeus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Frans David von Alopaeus, born on February 12, 1769, and passing on June 13, 1831, was a pivotal Russian diplomat of Finnish noble descent whose career spanned the tumultuous era of the Napoleonic Wars and the subsequent restructuring of Europe. As a member of the influential Alopaeus family, his diplomatic postings placed him at the heart of European power politics, particularly in Scandinavia and Central Europe. His contributions were instrumental in advancing Russian imperial interests during a period when the balance of power on the continent was constantly shifting, making him a significant, if often understated, figure in early 19th-century international relations.

Alopaeus served as the Russian envoy to Stockholm from 1803 to 1808, a critical period leading up to the Finnish War (1808–1809), which saw Sweden cede Finland to Russia. His role involved monitoring Swedish foreign policy and laying the groundwork for Russian strategic objectives in the Baltic region. Subsequently, he was appointed envoy to Berlin in 1808, where he remained until his death in 1831. During his long tenure in Prussia, Alopaeus navigated the complex Franco-Russian alliance, the subsequent Russian campaign of 1812, and the formation of the Sixth Coalition against Napoleon. He was instrumental in maintaining the fragile Prussian-Russian alliance and ensuring Prussian participation in the coalitions that ultimately led to Napoleon's downfall, thereby influencing the post-Napoleonic European order.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Frans David von Alopaeus held crucial diplomatic posts during the Napoleonic Wars, directly contributing to Russia's annexation of Finland and solidifying the Russo-Prussian alliance against Napoleon. His long tenure in Berlin was vital for maintaining Russian influence in Central Europe during a period of profound geopolitical change.
